text:
The taste of sugar is a deceptive simplicity: it begins with an immediate, sharp sweetness that hits the tongue like a promise, followed by a fleeting warmth that dissolves into nothingness, leaving behind only a hollow craving for more.

Liam stood before the canvas, the smell of turpentine and linseed oil thick in the air, but his mind was not on the swirling blues and grays he was mixing. It was on the ledger books waiting for him at the family’s textile mill. The conflict was no longer just a debate in the dining room; it had become a physical weight in his chest. His father’s voice, stern and unyielding, echoed in his head: "Art does not pay the bills, Liam. Duty does."

The tension snapped when Liam’s younger sister, Elena, burst into the studio, her face pale. "He’s sick," she whispered, her voice trembling. "Dad collapsed at the mill. The doctors say it’s stress, but they also say he needs to step down. He won’t listen. He’s trying to work through it."

Liam dropped his brush. The choice was no longer abstract. It was a triage of his soul. If he stayed true to his art, he would be abandoning his family in their hour of need, cementing the rift forever. If he returned to the mill, he would be suffocating the very spark that made him feel alive, turning his life into the same gray routine that had likely contributed to his father’s collapse.

He looked at the half-finished painting—a chaotic storm of colors representing his inner turmoil. Then he looked at the door leading out to the world, to the hospital, to the legacy he was expected to inherit. The sweetness of his passion was fading, replaced by the bitter, metallic taste of fear. He had to choose, and whatever he chose, a part of him would die.
